title: How Philippine local governments are navigating Super El Niño
summary: Local governments all over the country are deploying a mix of solutions to ensure water and energy remain accessible for farmlands and high-risk communities

blocks.text: CEBU, Philippines – Amid intense heat and dry weather, local government units (LGUs) in the Philippines are rolling out their own initiatives — from planting crop alternatives to water rationing — to minimize the impacts of the El Niño phenomenon.

As of November 5, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) announced that a very strong El Niño was present in the tropical Pacific Ocean and expected to persist until the first half of 2027.

According to PAGASA, the weather phenomenon will potentially reach its peak by the end of 2026, increasing the likelihood of rainfall deficits and, consequently, raising the odds of dry spells and drought in the country.

“Based on the latest drought assessment, five (5) provinces experienced meteorological drought, eleven (11) provinces were under dry spell, and ten (10) provinces experienced dry conditions in October 2026,” PAGASA Administrator Nathaniel Servando said in a statement.

At present, LGUs have begun forming special task forces and committees to supervise monitoring and mapping of high-risk areas, pursuant to directives from Malacañang and the Department of the Interior and Local Government.

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a meeting with government officials last November 4 that while some communities may face the risk of water shortages, others may lose electricity amid the intense heat.
Here’s how some LGUs in the regions are working through the very strong El Niño.
In Cebu, the provincial government is preparing for worst-case scenarios as El Niño could worsen its existing water shortage.

“We really lack infrastructure for water supply, and non-revenue water is also a problem. Most of the piping in the province needs repairs and maintenance,” Cebu Provincial Inter-LGU Water Systems Office (CPIWSO) Head Aldrin Barede told reporters on November 10.
In terms of mapping vulnerable communities, the Cebu Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office has identified a total of 183 barangays as high-risk areas.

“One of our interventions for this El Niño is water rationing. We are deploying water tanks to barangays, especially those in the mountains…. Aside from that, we are establishing water stations where LGU-owned water trucks can quickly refill,” Barede said.
Barede added that the province is fast-tracking the construction of its six water treatment plants — two are already completed and operating in Moalboal and Barili, respectively.

The province has identified at least seven major water sources: the Lusaran Weir and Buhisan Watershed in Cebu City, Mananga River in Talisay City and Minglanilla, Luyang Weir in Carmen, Cotcot Watershed in Liloan, Metro Cebu East Coast’s well fields, and the Mactan-Cordova desalination plant.
Mindanao’s energy sector faces a huge risk due to the fact that the region’s power generation mix enjoys a large contribution from its hydroelectric power plants.

Based on the Department of Energy’s data as of April 30, hydropower provides 1,059 megawatts in dependable capacity, which is around a 26% share of its power mix. This is second to coal’s contribution of 2,041 megawatts in dependable capacity, or around 50% of Mindanao’s power mix.

As river flows could potentially drop and affect hydroelectric power plant operations, local governments there are implementing load management and installing solar power systems in government buildings.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said in a November 10 presser that there could be a 60% reduction in the generation of hydropower plants and possible disruptions due to the heat.

In Iligan City, the local government requested the Power Sector Assets and Liabilities Management Corporation, National Power Corporation, Energy Regulatory Commission, and other concerned energy agencies to secure an allocation of 45 megawatts of power to the city.

“Considering Iligan City’s invaluable contribution to the energy sector as host of hydroelectric generating facilities, it is both equitable and reasonable that the City be afforded a preferential allocation of electric power for its own consumption and development,” the Iligan City legislative council’s Resolution No. 26-630 read.
Iligan hosts several facilities of the Agus Hydroelectric Power Plant Complex, which comprises six operating plants along the Agus River.
As of November 11, the Department of Agriculture reported that damage and losses due to the effects of El Niño reached nearly P10 billion, affecting more than 320,000 farmers.

The affected areas cover the Cordillera Administrative Region, Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, Bicol, Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Davao Region, Soccsksargen, and Caraga.
For Negros Occidental Governor Eugenio José Lacson, the biggest challenge for food security is making sure agricultural lands have proper irrigation amid low water levels.
“We hope to maintain the production, if not increase a little, at least maintain the production,” Lacson said in a November 5 interview.

Lacson, citing the provincial government’s experience in the previous 2023-2024 El Niño, said that their strategy is to ensure that farmers in areas that rely solely on rainfall would temporarily shift to more weather-resilient crops.
For non-irrigated lands, especially those that are near rivers, the Negros Occidental governor said that the province is aiming to install rubberized dams.

On November 4, the Batac City government in Ilocos Norte distributed 1,100 water pumps and 890 irrigation hoses to farmers in an effort to address crop damage caused by drought. The Office of the Provincial Agriculturist of Ilocos Norte reported earlier in November that several drought-affected areas were rice fields with no access to irrigation facilities.
Meanwhile, the deployment of solar-powered irrigation systems has ramped up in the northern provinces of Luzon.

In late October, the P1.49-billion Alfonso Lista Pump Irrigation System in Barangay Santo Domingo, Alfonso Lista, Ifugao, was formally inaugurated. The ALPIS is expected to increase crop yields on over 2,300 hectares of agricultural land.

In September, the Isabela provincial government, in collaboration with the DA, provided 130 solar-powered pumps and 40 mobile solar-powered water pumps for priority areas to help sustain farm operations during the dry spell. – Rappler.com
This story will be updated once we get more information from other local government units.
